rv.q: Underwood turns in a consummately empathetic, award-worthy portrayal of Ivanov.
This gripping adaptation captures the central insight of Chekhov’s first masterpiece: misunderstanding one another is both comic and calamitous.
One only wishes that the direction and acting in “The Real Ivanov” were as consistently, smoothly coordinated.
Strausfeld’s production has some brief, but strong visual moments and a few layered performances in supporting roles, but it did not unlock the play’s power for me.
Yet, in the end, I couldn't help but think that this is Ivanov delivered in rhetorical snippets and carefully curated snapshots.
But this is an enervated evening, bustling about without a clear purpose and filled with performances severely in need of editing.
Sadly (and not in a good way), The Real Ivanov does not resonate.
If only it was occasionally funny, it might have mitigated the despair I felt by the curtain call.
The production also conveys Chekhov's themes in ways that resonate with what we recognize as unchanging human nature.

Chekhov’s understanding of depression and social judgment remains remarkably contemporary; this production feels less timeless, and I suspect the problem is primarily one of direction rather than talent.
This Ivanov is out of place in his society, as well as in this muddled production.
This show is incredibly unique, strangely staged, and utterly unforgettable, even in depicting heavy subject matter.
Despite what I gather are adapter/director Laura Strausfeld's attempts, this production does not emerge comedic.
The Real Ivanov is a mere 100 minutes but felt like three hours.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Chekhov adaptation, with praise for Sam Underwood's performance but criticism of the confusing script and stark staging. Most find it more despairing than comedic, lacking the energy to justify its "Real" title.
